Field Memory in AI Ethics

How AI ethics remembers computer ethics, and the attributional afterlives of its canon, 2015–2025 · Deep Culture, University of Amsterdam

AI ethics grew quickly after 2015 and took a canon with it from computer ethics. On this site, we follow that canon through twelve venues and read it in two ways (Venturini, Jacomy and Jensen 2021).

Where the canon is remembered is read topologically, by regions: which venue groups cite which canonical works. How four claims travel is read diagrammatically, by following paths: whether later papers make each claim's argument, and whom they credit for it.

Read with careThis is not a map of influence. A line or a position records a documented citation or textual connection, not transmission. The corpus is bounded. It covers twelve venues, and its reference data is uneven by venue and year. The readings in the second part were made by AI readers. Every positive code was checked by a human reviewer, while most negative codes stand as the AI proposed them.

Four questions

Four questions that still structure debate. These are interpretive prompts for discussion, not summaries that exhaust the texts. Each card also shows where the work is remembered today.

Dates identify publications, not the origin of a problem. Rates are citing papers per 1,000 papers with reference data, 2015–2025.

Where the canon is remembered

Each dot is a corpus paper, placed by ForceAtlas2 from its whole reference list. The venue groups form overlapping regions. Pick a work in the chart to see where its citers sit. However, the comparison rests on the rates rather than on the layout.

Citing papers per 1,000 papers with reference data

The chart sets the journals against the FAccT group, with 95% intervals. We count a work as cited more in one group only when that holds under four checks: all links, curated records only, counts adjusted for detection, and each journal left out in turn. The four claims read in part two are in bold.

Two canons
3 · 7
works are cited more at FAccT (bias, accountability, due process) and in the journals (machine agency, moral status, responsibility for autonomous machines).
Machine learning
4 of 2,877
NeurIPS, ICML and ICLR ethics papers (2015–2021) cite any register work, against 823 papers in the journals and 140 in the FAccT group.
The bridge
896 · 148
citations between the FAccT group and the ML conferences, against those between the journals and the ML conferences. FAccT is the bridge, but the canon does not cross it.

How four claims travel

Every paper in the corpus that cites the claim and has a full text was read against a written statement of the claim, as was a matched set of uncited papers from the same venues and years.

What later papers do with the claim

Rows show what the paper's own argument does with the claim, and columns show how it attributes the claim. Each cell gives citing papers / matched uncited papers. Bold rows make the move.

Route map

The route map is read by following paths rather than by position. Faint lines link the claim directly to each later paper, coloured by how the paper attributes it. Strong lines are routes through intermediaries: thick lines were read on both sides, solid lines were read in the later paper, and dashed lines rest on bibliographic data only. The intermediary routes were prepared with AI assistance and have not been independently checked.
